prompt:
A *graph* consists of a set of vertices and a set of edges connecting pairs of vertices. If vertices $u$ and $v$ are connected by an edge, we say they are *adjacent*. The *degree* of a vertex $u$ is the number of vertices $v$ which are adjacent to $u$. A *finite* graph has a finite number of vertices. A *coloring* of a graph is an assignment of a color to each vertex of the graph. A coloring is *good* if no two adjacent vertices are the same color. The *chromatic number* of a graph is the minimum number of colors needed in any good coloring of that graph.

What are the chromatic numbers of each of the three graphs shown below? (In the original you also draw a minimum coloring for each.)

solutions.title: Read off each graph
solutions.body:
*Left (hexagon with a center joined to all six corners):* the center is adjacent to every corner, and the six corners form a cycle, so at least $1+2=3$ colors are needed (a triangle exists). Color the center with color $1$ and alternate $2,3,2,3,2,3$ around the even hexagon. So $\chi=3$.

*Middle (five vertices, all pairs adjacent, i.e. $K_5$):* all five vertices must have different colors, so $\chi=5$.

*Right (a tree):* a tree has an edge, so $\chi\ge2$, and any tree can be $2$-colored (color vertices by the parity of their distance from a fixed vertex). So $\chi=2$.

**Answer: $3$, $5$, $2$**

In a *connected* graph, it is possible to reach any vertex from any other vertex by following the edges. A *tree* is a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $n-1$ edges for some positive integer $n$. Suppose $n\ge2$. What is the chromatic number of a tree having $n$ vertices? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Induction removing a leaf
solutions.body:
At least $2$ colors are needed since a tree with $n\ge2$ vertices has an edge. We show every tree can be $2$-colored by induction on $n$. For $n=2$ it is clear. A tree with $n\ge3$ vertices has a leaf $\ell$ (a vertex of degree $1$): a connected graph with $n-1$ edges has degrees summing to $2(n-1)<2n$, so some vertex has degree at most $1$, and connectedness with $n\ge2$ makes it exactly $1$. Removing $\ell$ leaves a connected graph with $n-1$ vertices and $n-2$ edges, which is a tree; $2$-color it by induction. Give $\ell$ the color different from that of its unique neighbour. This is a good $2$-coloring. So the chromatic number is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

Let $n\ge3$ be a positive integer. A *triangulation* of a convex $n$-gon is a set of $n-3$ of its diagonals which do not intersect in the interior of the polygon. Along with the $n$ sides, these diagonals separate the polygon into $n-2$ disjoint triangles. Any triangulation can be viewed as a graph: the vertices of the graph are the corners of the polygon, and the $n$ sides and $n-3$ diagonals are the edges.

For a fixed $n$-gon, different triangulations correspond to different graphs. Prove that all of these graphs have the same chromatic number.
answer: All triangulation graphs have chromatic number $3$.

Let $G$ be a finite graph in which every vertex has degree less than or equal to $k$. Prove that the chromatic number of $G$ is less than or equal to $k+1$.
answer: Greedy coloring uses at most $k+1$ colors.

solutions.title: Greedy coloring
solutions.body: List the vertices $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and color them in order, giving each the smallest of the colors $1,\dots,k+1$ not already used on one of its neighbours that were colored earlier. Each vertex has at most $k$ neighbours, so at most $k$ of the $k+1$ colors are blocked, and a free color always exists. The result is a good coloring with at most $k+1$ colors. ∎

A *coloring* of a graph is an assignment of a color to each vertex of the graph. A coloring is *good* if no two adjacent vertices are the same color. The *chromatic number* of a graph is the minimum number of colors needed in any good coloring of that graph.

A *$k$-clique* of a graph is a set of $k$ vertices such that all pairs of vertices in the clique are adjacent. The *clique number* of a graph is the size of the largest clique in the graph. Does there exist a graph which has a clique number smaller than its chromatic number?

solutions.title: The 5-cycle
solutions.body:
Yes. Take the cycle on $5$ vertices $x_0,\dots,x_4$, with $x_i$ adjacent to $x_{i\pm1}$ (indices mod $5$). No three vertices are pairwise adjacent and there is an edge, so the clique number is $2$. Two colors are not enough: the colors would have to alternate around the cycle, which is impossible for an odd cycle. Three colors suffice ($1,2,1,2,3$). So the chromatic number is $3>2$.

**Answer: Yes**

A *coloring* of a graph is an assignment of a color to each vertex of the graph. A coloring is *good* if no two adjacent vertices are the same color. The *chromatic number* of a graph is the minimum number of colors needed in any good coloring of that graph.

If a single vertex is removed from a finite graph, show that the graph's chromatic number cannot decrease by more than $1$.
answer: If $\chi(G-v)\le\chi(G)-2$, give $v$ a new color to get a coloring of $G$ with fewer than $\chi(G)$ colors.

solutions.title: Add the vertex back
solutions.body: Let $G$ have chromatic number $C$ and let $v$ be a vertex. Suppose $G-v$ could be colored with at most $C-2$ colors. Give $v$ a color not used in that coloring. This is a good coloring of $G$ (the new color appears only on $v$) with at most $C-1$ colors, contradicting $\chi(G)=C$. So $\chi(G-v)\ge C-1$. ∎

The *chromatic number* of a graph is the minimum number of colors needed in any good coloring of that graph.

Show that, for any $n>2$, there are infinitely many graphs with chromatic number $n$ such that removing any vertex (and all its incident edges) from the graph decreases its chromatic number.
answer: Join an odd cycle $C_k$ ($k$ any odd number) with $K_{n-3}$.

solutions.title: Odd cycle joined with a clique
solutions.body:
For each odd $k\ge3$ let $C_k$ be the cycle on $k$ vertices, with $\chi(C_k)=3$. Let $H=K_{n-3}$ (empty if $n=3$) and let $J_k$ be the graph with vertex set $C_k\cup H$, all edges of $C_k$ and $H$, and every edge between a vertex of $C_k$ and a vertex of $H$. The graphs $J_k$ are pairwise different (they have different numbers of vertices), so there are infinitely many.

*$\chi(J_k)=n$:* the $n-3$ vertices of $H$ are adjacent to everything, so they receive $n-3$ distinct colors that appear nowhere else, while $C_k$ needs $3$ further colors. Thus at least $n$ colors are needed and $(n-3)+3=n$ suffice.

*Removing a vertex lowers $\chi$:* removing a vertex of $C_k$ turns the cycle into a path, which is $2$-colorable, so $(n-3)+2=n-1$ colors suffice. Removing a vertex of $H$ leaves $K_{n-4}$ joined to $C_k$, which needs $(n-4)+3=n-1$ colors. Either way the chromatic number drops below $n$ (by exactly $1$). ∎
